beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Night three. Twelve wolves. One fire. And it's burning out.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: The biggest one steps into the light. And Maya whispers. Don't run.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Four days earlier, you were on a plane.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: This is Your Move. Ten choices. Pause the video, pick your move, and keep count. Get them right, and you walk off this mountain.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Flight two eleven. Thirty eight thousand feet over the Rocky Mountains. You're halfway through a movie.

beats.name: RADIO
beats.text: Ladies and gentlemen, we've lost an engine. Please return to your seats and fasten your seatbelts.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Then the second engine goes quiet. And the oxygen masks drop.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Out the window there are no clouds anymore. Just trees. Getting closer, fast.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: Heads down! Brace! Brace! Brace!

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your bag is right above you. Your phone, your jacket, everything you brought.

beats.opt1: Grab your bag from the bin
beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Grab your bag? Or get your head down?

beats.opt1: Grab your bag from the bin

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you grabbed your bag, you're standing when the plane hits the trees. You don't remember the next hour.

paper.title: BRACE POSITION
paper.src: FAA passenger safety guidance on brace positions

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: In a crash, the brace position protects your head from flying debris and the seat in front of you. Bags can be replaced. Heads can't.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you braced, good move. You feel the belly of the plane scrape the treetops. Then the whole world goes white.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You wake up face down in the snow. The plane is in two pieces. And the back half is on fire.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Someone is still inside. The flight attendant. Maya.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You drag her out by the jacket, ten seconds before the fuel tank goes up.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: Thank you. I'm Maya. Is anyone else...?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Her leg is cut. Not deep, but she can only limp.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You check what you have. A lighter. A water bottle. And from the plane's emergency kit, one red flare. Remember that flare.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Nobody else. Just the two of you, somewhere in the mountains. And the sun goes down in one hour.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Far below, you think you can see a road. Maybe. It's a long way down.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Walk down the mountain to find help? Or stay with the wreck?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you walked, night catches you halfway down. In the dark, every slope looks the same. You're lost, and nobody knows where to look.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: In the morning, rescuers reach the wreck in twenty minutes. It takes them three days to find you.

paper.title: STAY WITH THE WRECK
paper.src: standard aviation search and rescue advice

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Search teams look for the wreck first. From the air, a plane is huge. A person is a dot.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you stayed, good move. The front half still has walls and a roof. That's your shelter tonight.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Night one. Your lips are cracking. You haven't had a drink since the plane.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: And you're sitting on a mountain made of water.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: We could just eat the snow, right?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Eat the snow? Or melt it first?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you ate it, your body burns its own heat to melt every mouthful. Ten minutes later, you're shaking. Hard.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Eating snow lowers your body temperature and costs you energy you can't spare. Always melt it first.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you melted it, good move. A water bottle from the plane, held over the fire. Warm water. The best thing you've ever tasted.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: The rule of threes. Three hours without shelter in this cold. Three days without water. You've solved both. For now.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Somewhere far off, something howls. Then another. Maya pretends she didn't hear it.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Morning. Day two. You hear it before you see it. An engine. A search helicopter.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: It's high. It's fast. And it's about to fly right past you.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: Wave! Make them see us!

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You have maybe thirty seconds before it's over the next ridge and gone.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Build three signal fires? Or jump, wave and scream?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you waved, you're a dot in the snow, waving its arms. From the air, you look like a rock. The helicopter flies on.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Three of anything is the signal for distress. Three fires. Three whistles. Three piles of rocks. And on snow, dark smoke stands out.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you built three fires and threw seat foam on them for black smoke, good move. The helicopter banks. It circles once. It saw you.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Maya runs to the cockpit radio. It crackles to life.

beats.name: RADIO
beats.text: Survivors spotted. Storm incoming. Earliest rescue is forty eight hours.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: The storm hits like a wall. Sixty mile an hour winds. You can't see your own feet.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: The wreck is groaning in the wind. Three hundred yards away, there's a line of trees. Real shelter.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Walk to the trees through the whiteout? Or dig in where you are?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you walked, you walk for an hour. And end up right back at the wreck. You walked in a circle.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: And you've burned an hour of body heat you'll never get back.

paper.title: WHITEOUT
paper.src: Souman et al., Current Biology (2009): people walk in circles without visual cues

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: In a whiteout, people walk in circles. With no landmarks, nobody walks straight. Scientists have actually tested it.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you dug in, good move. A trench in the snow behind the wreck, lined with seat cushions. Snow is one of the best insulators on Earth.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: At midnight, Maya stops talking. Her lips are blue. And she's stopped shivering.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Shivering is your body fighting the cold. When it stops, the fight is being lost. You pull her close and share your heat until she starts shaking again.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: The storm screams all night. By morning, the wreck is gone. Buried under six feet of snow.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Quick check. Halfway through. If you're five for five, don't get cocky. Chapter eight gets almost everybody.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Day three. The radio is buried with the wreck. If you want to be found, you have to get lower. Down to the valley.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Straight down the open slope is twenty minutes. Along the rocky ridge, it's two hours.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: The slope's faster. I'm freezing. Let's go.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. The fast open slope? Or the long ridge?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you took the slope, halfway down you hear a crack. Like a gunshot. Then the whole hill starts to move.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You dive behind a boulder. The snow roars past for ten seconds. Then silence. Maya is gone.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Most avalanches happen on slopes between thirty and forty five degrees. And fresh snow from a storm makes it far worse.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you took the ridge, good move. Two hours in, you hear the crack anyway. And watch the slope you almost took slide away below you.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: We would have been under that.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: By noon, you reach the valley floor. And a frozen river blocks the way.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: The ice looks solid. It's twenty steps across. On the other side, the forest looks a lot like a way out.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: My leg can't do two more hours of this.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Follow the river downstream? Or walk across the ice?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you crossed, step fifteen goes straight through. The water is so cold it knocks the air out of your lungs.

paper.title: THE ICE RULE
paper.src: ice safety guidance (e.g. Minnesota DNR) + cold-water 1-10-1 principle

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Ice over moving water is thinner, and you can't tell by looking. You need at least four inches of solid ice. And remember the cold water rule. One minute of shock. Ten before your arms quit.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you followed the river, good move. Rivers run downhill. And downhill is where people live.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: An hour later, you find old tire tracks along the bank, half filled with snow. Somebody drove here. Once.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: But by sunset, there's still no town. And it's starting to snow again.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You find a cave in the rocks. Out of the wind. Maya almost cries.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your legs feel like concrete. Your stomach stopped growling yesterday. That's not a good sign. But it's not the thing that kills you.

paper.title: THE RULE OF THREES
paper.src: the survival rule of threes (rough guide)

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You can survive about three weeks without food. Cold and thirst will get you long before hunger does.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: And the cave goes deep. It's warmer further in. Way warmer.

beats.opt2: Stay by the entrance with a fire
beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Sleep deep inside the cave? Or stay by the entrance with a fire?

beats.opt2: Stay by the entrance with a fire

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you went deep, that warm air is coming from something breathing. Something big. And it just woke up.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You back out slowly, never turning your back on it. It doesn't follow you. This time.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Warm, quiet caves are exactly where bears sleep through winter. Stay near the entrance, where you can see out and get out.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you stayed by the entrance, good move. Fire in the cave mouth, smoke drifting out, warmth bouncing off the rock. You sleep for the first time in two days.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Then, at two in the morning, Maya shakes you awake. Eyes. Outside. A lot of eyes.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Twelve wolves. One fire. And it's burning out. You've seen this before.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: The biggest one steps into the light.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: Don't run. Please. Don't run.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Their breath steams in the firelight. You can hear them breathing.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Stand tall and make noise? Or run for the trees?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you ran, you just told twelve hunters you're prey. Wolves chase whatever runs. And in deep snow, they are much faster than you.

paper.title: THE PREDATOR RULE
paper.src: wildlife agency guidance on wolf encounters

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Never run from a predator. Make yourself big, make noise, and keep the fire between you. Wolf attacks on people are rare. Running makes one far more likely.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you stood your ground, good move. You throw the last branch on the fire, raise your arms, and roar. Maya bangs two pieces of the plane together.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: It lasts eleven minutes. The longest eleven minutes of your life.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: One by one, the eyes slide back into the dark.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Day four. Dawn. You have one thing left from the plane. A single emergency flare.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Then you hear it. Rotors. Far away, somewhere behind the ridge.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: Light it! Light it now!

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Your move. Light the flare now? Or wait until you can see the helicopter?

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you lit it now, a hand flare burns for about a minute. The helicopter clears the ridge two minutes later. Your flare is ash.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You hear it pass overhead, behind the trees. You scream until your voice cracks. It never sees you.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: A hand flare burns for about one minute. Save it until the aircraft can actually see you.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: If you waited, good move. The helicopter clears the ridge. You light the flare and hold it over your head. Bright red light. Red smoke.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: It turns. It's coming straight for you.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Fifty seconds of flare left. Forty. The pilot dips the nose.

beats.name: RADIO
beats.text: We see you. Hold your position. We're coming down.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: A rescuer drops down on a cable, grabs Maya first, then you. The ground falls away below your boots.

beats.name: MAGS
beats.text: Maya grabs your hand and yells over the rotors. Your move. Every single time.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: You made it. Four days. Ten moves. Two people walked off that mountain.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Back home, the news calls it a miracle. It wasn't a miracle. It was ten good moves.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Now count your moves. Ten out of ten, you're a legend. Seven or more, you survived. Under five, you're wolf food.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: Comment your score. And subscribe, because your next move is coming.

beats.name: NARRATOR
beats.text: And tell me which move almost got you.
